title: The Road to the Civil War
summary: Follow the chain of conflicts over slavery's expansion from 1850 to 1861 and decide which link did the most to make war unavoidable.
challenge: The Civil War did not begin with a single event. Through the 1850s, a chain of conflicts over whether slavery could expand into the western territories pushed the nation toward war — each action producing a sharper reaction. Trace the chain from pressure to consequence, and decide which link mattered most.

links.textKey: Disputes over whether slavery may expand into western territories won from Mexico (1848–1850).
Compromise of 1850 and its Fugitive Slave Act (Sept. 1850) — a deal that also forced free states to return escaped people.
Kansas–Nebraska Act (May 1854) reopens the question by 'popular sovereignty,' leading to 'Bleeding Kansas' violence (1854–1859).
Dred Scott decision (March 1857) denies Black citizenship and any federal power to bar slavery; John Brown's Harpers Ferry raid (Oct. 1859) hardens both sides.
Lincoln's election (Nov. 1860) leads Deep South states to secede (Dec. 1860–Feb. 1861); Confederates fire on Fort Sumter (April 12–14, 1861).
Outbreak of the Civil War (1861–1865); the Upper South secedes after Sumter; the war becomes one that ends slavery.

mapData.altKey: What if the Compromise of 1850 had not included the harsh Fugitive Slave Act — would sectional anger have cooled instead of spreading North?
people: Stephen A. Douglas — authored the Kansas–Nebraska Act and popular sovereignty
Chief Justice Roger B. Taney — wrote the Dred Scott majority opinion
John Brown — led the Harpers Ferry raid
Abraham Lincoln — whose election triggered secession
mapData.mostKey: Which single link did the most to make war unavoidable — the Fugitive Slave Act, the Kansas–Nebraska Act, Dred Scott, Harpers Ferry, or Lincoln's election? Choose one, and use evidence from at least two other links to defend it.

teacherText.keyideas: Slavery — and specifically whether it could expand into new territories — was the central cause of the sectional crisis. Each compromise or ruling meant to settle the question instead sharpened it: the Fugitive Slave Act angered the North, the Kansas–Nebraska Act reopened the territories, Dred Scott denied any federal limit on slavery, and Lincoln's election (on a platform opposing slavery's expansion) triggered secession and war.
teacherText.misconceptions:
• The war's central cause was slavery, not merely 'states' rights' in the abstract.
• The Compromise of 1850 did not settle the issue; its Fugitive Slave Act inflamed it.
• Lincoln's 1860 platform opposed the expansion of slavery, not (yet) its immediate abolition everywhere.
